'''William Arthur Little''' (born 17 November 1930) is a South African-born American physicist and Professor Emeritus at [[Stanford University]], specializing in [[condensed matter physics]]. He is also the chairman of two manufacturing companies that he co-founded.

== Early life and academic career ==
Little was born in [[Adelaide, South Africa]] on 17 November 1930. He graduated from the [[University of South Africa]] in 1950 and then received two PhD degrees, one from [[Rhodes University]] in 1955 and the other from the [[University of Glasgow]] in 1957.<ref name="USA">{{Cite book |title = American Men & Women of Science |editor=Jaques Cattell Press |publisher = R. R. Bowker Co. |edition = 16th|volume = IV|year=1986| page = 809 }}</ref><ref name="WHO">{{cite web|url=https://whoswhonewsletters.com/2018/09/05/william-little/|title=WILLIAM A LITTLE|date=5 September 2018|website=[[Marquis Who's Who]]|accessdate=2 October 2026}}</ref>

He worked for the [[National Research Council Canada]] as a postdoctoral fellow from 1956 to 1958. He then served as an assistant and associate professor at [[Stanford University]] from 1958 to 1965 and as a professor from 1965 until his retirement in 1994, after which he became an emeritus professor at the university.<ref name="USA"/><ref name="WHO"/>

During his academic career, he held the fellowships from the [[Alfred P. Sloan Foundation]] from 1959 to 1962, and from the [[John Simon Guggenheim Memorial Foundation]] from 1964 to 1965. He also served as a visiting professor at the [[University of Geneva]] from 1964 to 1965, and as a senior fellow at the [[National Science Foundation]] from 1971 to 1972.<ref name="USA"/>

== Business career ==
Since retiring, Little has shifted his focus towards managing MMR Technologies Inc., which he co-founded in 1980. The company produces cryogenic equipment and instruments for materials science, including micro-miniature refrigerators, office [[liquid nitrogen]] generators, and [[cryocoolers]] used with X-ray and gamma-ray detectors. In 1999, he also co-founded 3L&T, Inc., which specializes in the development of polymer material technologies and provides [[corrosion]] protection coatings and linings for industrial plants.<ref name="WHO"/>

== Research ==
His research has focused on low-temperature physics, [[superconductivity]], and [[neural network]] theory.<ref name="USA"/>

In 1962, Little and Ronald D. Parks conducted experiments involving empty and thin-walled superconducting cylinders that were subjected to a parallel magnetic field.<ref>{{cite journal|title=Observation of Quantum Periodicity in the Transition Temperature of a Superconducting Cylinder|author1=W. A. Little|author2=R. D. Parks|journal=[[Physical Review Letters]]|volume=9|page=9|year=1962|doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.9.9}}</ref> They observed periodic oscillations in electronic resistance in relation to the magnetic flux, which is now known as the [[Little–Parks effect]]. This means the quantization of the flux, and is one of the early experimental evidences of the formation of [[Cooper pairs]] in the [[BCS theory]].<ref>{{cite journal| title=Magnetic flux periodicity of h/e in superconducting loops|author1=F. Loder|author2=A. P. Kampf|author3=T. Kopp|author4=J. Mannhart|author5=C. W. Schneider|author6=Y. S. Barash |journal=[[Nature Physics]]|volume=4|pages=112–115|year=2008|doi= 10.1038/nphys813|arxiv= 0709.4111v2|bibcode= 2008NatPh...4..112L}}</ref>

In 1964, he proposed a superconducting mechanism based on the electronic excitation of polarizable molecules, such as conductive polyene spines, and predicted that the critical temperature would exceed room temperature by a large margin.<ref>{{cite journal|last=Little|first=W. A. |title=Possibility of Synthesizing an Organic Superconductor|journal=Physical Review|volume=134|pages=A1416-A1424|year=1964|doi=10.1103/PhysRev.134.A1416|bibcode=1964PhRv..134.1416L}}</ref> This report attracted many physicists and chemists, facilitating the theoretical study of excitonic superconductivity and the synthesis of [[organic conductor]]s and [[organic superconductors|superconductors]].<ref>{{Cite journal|first=Denis|last=Jerome|author-link= Denis Jérome|title=William A. Little: Who shook up superconductivity|journal=MRS Bulletin|volume=50|pages=1269-1273|doi=10.1557/s43577-025-01014-6|doi-access=free}}</ref>

== Awards ==
Little was elected a Fellow of the [[American Physical Society]] in 1961.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.aps.org/funding-recognition/aps-fellowship?q=william%20little&af=true|title=Search Results for William Little|website=APS Fellows Archive|accessdate=2 October 2026}}</ref>

In 2006, he received an [[R&D]] 100 Award for air-liquid nitrogen products developed by his company.<ref>{{cite web|url= https://www.rdworldonline.com/rd-100-archive//?YEAR=2006 |title= R&D 100 Archive of Winners in 2006|website=R&D World|accessdate=2 October 2026}}</ref> He was awarded the [[Samuel C. Collins]] Award in 2007 and the [[Albert Nelson Marquis]] Lifetime Achievement Award in 2017.<ref name="WHO"/><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.cec-icmc.org/2025/cec-collins-award/|title=CEC – Samuel C. Collins Award|website=CEC/ICMC 2025|accessdate=2 October 2026}}</ref>
